reference.source: Williams Textbook of Endocrinology / Nelson Textbook of Pediatrics
clinicalPearls: A disorder of end-organ resistance to parathyroid hormone rather than a deficiency of the hormone itself
Biochemically characterised by hypocalcaemia and hyperphosphataemia with an elevated PTH, the opposite of hypoparathyroidism
Caused by defects in GNAS, which encodes the stimulatory G-protein alpha subunit coupling receptors to adenylate cyclase
Subtype 1A is associated with the Albright hereditary osteodystrophy phenotype, including short stature, rounded face, and shortened metacarpals
Resistance may extend to other Gs-coupled hormones, producing features such as hypothyroidism from TSH resistance
Parental origin of the mutation influences the phenotype because GNAS is subject to tissue-specific imprinting
Pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism shares the physical phenotype but has normal calcium biochemistry
reference.pathophysiology: Parathyroid hormone acts through a receptor that signals via the stimulatory G-protein to generate cyclic AMP in target tissues such as kidney and bone. In pseudohypoparathyroidism, GNAS mutations impair this Gs-alpha signalling, so target organs fail to respond to PTH despite adequate or elevated hormone levels. The renal resistance reduces calcium reabsorption and phosphate excretion, producing hypocalcaemia and hyperphosphataemia, while the low calcium drives compensatory secondary rises in PTH. Because GNAS is imprinted, the parent from whom the mutation is inherited determines whether multi-hormone resistance and the osteodystrophy phenotype are expressed.
additionalDifferentials: Chronic kidney disease with secondary hyperparathyroidism
Other causes of hypocalcaemia such as hypomagnesaemia
additionalInvestigations: Serum calcium, phosphate and intact parathyroid hormone demonstrating PTH resistance
Serum magnesium and vitamin D metabolites to exclude other causes of hypocalcaemia
Thyroid function tests to detect associated TSH resistance
Molecular genetic and methylation analysis of the GNAS locus
Radiographs of the hands to identify shortened metacarpals and other skeletal features
redFlags: Symptomatic hypocalcaemia with tetany, laryngospasm or seizures requiring urgent correction
Prolonged QT interval on the electrocardiogram from severe hypocalcaemia
Features of resistance to multiple hormones indicating broad Gs-alpha involvement
Ectopic ossification or other complications requiring specialist assessment
reference.prognosis: With calcium and active vitamin D therapy guided by PTH and calcium targets, biochemical control and symptom prevention are generally achievable, although the skeletal phenotype and any additional hormone resistance persist and require ongoing management.
pitfalls: Mistaking the high-PTH, low-calcium pattern for secondary hyperparathyroidism of renal disease
Confusing pseudohypoparathyroidism with pseudopseudohypoparathyroidism, which has normal calcium
Overlooking coexisting hormone resistance such as subclinical hypothyroidism
Aiming for high-normal calcium and risking hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis
management: Restore calcium with oral calcium supplementation and an active vitamin D analogue such as calcitriol or alfacalcidol, titrated to calcium and PTH targets
Moderate dietary phosphate to help control hyperphosphataemia while avoiding ectopic calcification
Screen for and treat additional hormone resistance, notably hypothyroidism from TSH resistance, with levothyroxine
Monitor serum calcium, phosphate, PTH and urinary calcium, and the renal tract for calcification
Manage the Albright hereditary osteodystrophy features such as short stature and obesity
Genetic counselling with attention to imprinting and parent-of-origin effects, and family evaluation
